question: What does f do to very simple, varied single inputs (lowercase word, uppercase word, digits, single characters, spaces, punctuation)?
expect: No model yet, so this is a broad first look. Likely outcomes: if outputs equal inputs, f may be identity on these; if case changes, I'll see which direction (upper/lower); if digits or symbols vanish/transform, that reveals filtering or mapping; empty string output tells me how f handles no input; mixed alphanumeric shows whether operations apply per-character or to the whole string. Each distinct pattern (identity vs. case-flip vs. stripping vs. reversal) will pin down the first basic operation to model.

question: Does the first-character capitalization apply to the first non-space character after spaces are removed, or to the literal first character of the original string (so a leading space would prevent capitalization)?
expect: If spaces are removed first and then the first remaining character is capitalized, we get 'Hello','Hello','A1b2','123','!abc','','Helloworld','Helloworld','Abc','A'. If instead capitalization is applied to the literal first character before/without regard to leading spaces, leading-space inputs would stay lowercase like ' hello' -> 'hello' or ' a1B2' -> 'a1b2', and '  A' might become 'a'. This distinguishes the two hypotheses and also checks whether all spaces (including internal multiple spaces) are removed and how mixed-case words behave.

question: Does f treat only the ASCII space character as removable, or does it also remove other whitespace (tab, newline) and/or collapse internal spaces, and does capitalization depend on the literal first character being a space vs. other whitespace?
expect: If f only strips ASCII spaces, tabs/newlines remain: outputs like 'Hello' (if leading tab doesn't block cap) or 'hello' with a literal tab, 'Hello\tworld'/'Helloworld' depending on tab handling, and 'A b' with NBSP kept. If f removes all whitespace, tabs/newlines/NBSP vanish and results look like space-removed cases. Comparing 'a b' vs 'a\tb' vs 'a\u00a0b' isolates which characters are removed; '\t hello' vs ' hello\tworld' shows whether non-space leading whitespace blocks capitalization.

question: Does the capitalization rule look only at the literal first character being whitespace, or does it depend on the first character of the whitespace-stripped string being a letter (so leading punctuation/digits also prevent capitalization)?
expect: If capitalization depends only on the original first char not being whitespace, outputs would be: !abc, 1abc, _abc, .abc, -abc, !abc, 1abc, !hello, !!!a, !abc (i.e. first char after stripping is capitalized regardless of whether it's a letter — but since these already start with punctuation/digits, no visible change). If instead f capitalizes the first letter anywhere in the result, outputs would be: !Abc, 1Abc, _Abc, .Abc, -Abc, !Abc, 1Abc, !Hello, !!!A, !Abc. This distinguishes 'capitalize first char only if it's the literal first char and non-space' from 'capitalize first alphabetic char' and also tests whether leading whitespace blocks capitalization when followed by punctuation.

question: Does capitalization depend on the original first character being whitespace, or on the first character of the stripped string being a letter (so leading non-letter symbols/digits/whitespace prevent capitalization)?
expect: Model v3 predicts ['_hello','.hello','-hello','1hello','!hello','hello','_hello','1hello','!hello','hello'] (capitalize only when stripped result starts with a letter and original doesn't start with whitespace). If instead outputs are ['_Hello','.Hello','-Hello','1Hello','!Hello','hello','_Hello','1Hello','!Hello','hello'], then capitalization is based only on non-whitespace first char and applies to any character that can be uppercased (though symbols/digits can't), confirming the 'letter-start' rule; any divergence on '\nhello' tests whether newline counts as whitespace for the capitalization guard.

question: Does the capitalization rule apply only to ASCII lowercase letters a-z (so non-ASCII letters like é/ü are not uppercased), and how are non-ASCII letters treated overall?
expect: If capitalization only uppercases ASCII a-z, then 'éclair' stays 'éclair' (first char é not uppercased), 'über' stays 'über', while 'aé' becomes 'Aé' and '1é' stays '1é'. If Unicode-aware capitalization is used, 'éclair' would become 'Éclair' and 'über' would become 'Über'. 'ÉCLAIR' and 'ÜBER' will lowercase to 'éclair'/'über' either way; 'straße' will lowercase to 'straße' (or 'strasse' if a special case-mapping is used, which would be a distinct signal). This separates ASCII-only capitalization from full Unicode capitalization and checks whether lowercasing is plain per-character lowercase.

question: How does f handle non-ASCII whitespace-like characters (e.g. non-breaking space U+00A0, em space U+2003) — are they removed like ASCII whitespace, and do they block capitalization if they are the first character?
expect: If only ASCII whitespace is stripped (as E3's a\u00a0b -> Ab suggests removal of NBSP, but this needs confirmation), outputs would be lowercase with NBSP/em-space removed: 'ab', 'abc', 'ab', 'abc', etc. If non-ASCII spaces are kept literally, we'd see 'a\u00a0b', '\u00a0abc', etc. Capitalization results distinguish whether a leading non-ASCII space blocks the first-letter uppercase (e.g. 'abc' vs 'Abc').

question: Does the capitalization rule apply to the first character of the whitespace-stripped string even when the original string has leading whitespace (i.e., is capitalization blocked by leading whitespace, or does it apply to the first surviving letter regardless of position)?

If capitalization instead applies to the first surviving letter after stripping whitespace, outputs starting with a letter will be capitalized (e.g., 'Abc', 'Éclair', 'A'). Mixed results will reveal whether only ASCII whitespace vs. all whitespace blocks capitalization, and whether the block depends on the original first char being whitespace or on the stripped string's first char being a letter.

question: Does f treat other Unicode whitespace/control characters (U+2000 en quad, U+2028 line separator, U+2029 paragraph separator, U+0085 NEL, U+000C form feed, U+001C-U+001F file/group/record/unit separators) as removable whitespace, and do they block capitalization as first character?

question: Does f lowercase non-ASCII uppercase letters (e.g. É, Ü, Ñ) the way it lowercases ASCII letters, and does the capitalize-first-character rule then re-uppercase the first character — i.e. is lowercasing Unicode-aware rather than ASCII-only?

question: Does the capitalize-first rule uppercase the first surviving character when it is a digit or punctuation followed by a letter (i.e., is only a lowercase letter ever uppercased, or is the first character case-transformed regardless of type), and how are multi-character case mappings like ß handled mid-string?
